brief_context: Site of the first Thanksgiving in 1621.
brief_extract:
Whilst harvest thanksgiving celebrations were undoubtedly a part of the Pilgrim tradition, it is generally believed that the first Thanksgiving Day was celebrated in America when Governor William Bradford proclaimed a three-day festival in the autumn of 1621 to give thanks for the harvest. On that occasion, the Pilgrims in the tiny Plymouth Colony made their way to their Meeting House where they gave thanks, not just for the harvest but also for their survival through their first year of hard-won religious freedom. Bountiful harvest
In a letter of 11th December 1621, Edward Winslow wrote: "Our harvest being gotten in, our Governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a more special manner rejoice together, after we had gathered the fruit of our labours.

location_standardised: Plymouth, Plymouth County, Massachusetts, United States

brief_extract: This painting (by George H. Boughton in 1867) depicts a scene in the tiny Plymouth Colony on the morning of that first Thanksgiving Day. It shows the Pilgrims, the first settlers in New England, making their way to the meeting house to give thanks to God for a bountiful harvest.

brief_context: Source of original colonists' stores.
brief_extract: Plymouth at that time was just a small cluster of huts built mainly of turf and thatch. The colonists had few utensils and their stores brought from England were almost exhausted. The meal they shared with the Indians was probably limited to fish and game, including the deer contributed by the guests, served with corn and beans cooked in the Indian style.

But despite that early celebration of 1621, Thanksgiving Day was not established in America as a national event until more than two hundred years later and only at the end of the 18th century was Thanksgiving Day instituted throughout New Eng-land. George Washington proclaimed 26th November 1789 as the first National Day of Thanksgiving, but still the idea did not catch on.

Credit for the ultimate establishment of Thanksgiving Day is generally given to the efforts of Sarah J Hale, editor and founder in 1828 of the 'Ladies Magazine' published in Boston. Her editorials and her letters to President Lincoln resulted in his proclamation in 1863 and those of succeeding Presidents, but it was not until 1941 that the holiday was finally fixed by Congress to take place annually on the fourth Thursday in November.

brief_context: Region where Carolyn Berlin grew up.
brief_extract:
Family celebration
Coming, as she did, from the heart of the 'corn belt', Carolyn has vivid recollections of the old tradition, carried on by her Grandmother, of drying corn. "The Thanksgiving meal was wonderful," she told me, "everybody in the family cooked and they all brought something along with them; besides the turkey, cranberries, pumpkin pie and all the trimmings, we always had corn of some sort - a tradition which came originally from the Indians for whom it was a staple food, along with pumpkin and beans." She explained how the Pennsylvania Dutch in the Middle West had devised a method of preserving dried corn in jars for winter use; and she recalled how reconstituted corn kernels were always served at her family's Thanksgiving dinner. We talked about the traditional dishes which go to make up the Thanksgiving feast of turkey and garnishes (particularly cranberry sauce); mashed turnips; corn and beans (often served as 'succotash', an Indian word for dried corn made into a mush with water and with beans then added); relishes; pumpkin and mincemeat pies; and, finally, nuts and fruit.
